topic.name: Osteoarthritis
objectives: Differentiate OA from RA, gout, and pseudogout
Recognize classic X-ray findings of OA
Master stepwise pain management (non-pharm → topical → oral → injection)
Know joint injection indications, technique, and contraindications
Identify when to refer for joint replacement

content_chunks.title: Why This Matters
content_chunks.content: Meet Robert: 68, retired carpenter, knees creak like an old door. He's been using OTC ibuprofen for 2 years. Now his stomach hurts. His wife says he's limping more, and he can't get down on the floor to play with grandkids. He's tried glucosamine (did nothing) and now wants 'something stronger.' OA affects 32 million US adults — #1 cause of disability in the elderly. It's one of the most common conditions you'll manage in primary care, and the FNP boards WILL test you on differentiating it from inflammatory arthritis and choosing the right stepwise treatment.
content_chunks.visual_desc: X-ray showing joint space narrowing with osteophytes (bone spurs) at the medial knee compartment

content_chunks.title: What IS Osteoarthritis?
content_chunks.content:
**OA** = **Degenerative** joint disease — progressive **cartilage loss** over time.

**Pathophysiology**:
1. Mechanical stress + aging → cartilage breakdown
2. **Chondrocytes** try to repair but can't keep up
3. Cartilage wears away → **bone rubs on bone**
4. Body responds with **osteophytes** (bone spurs) and **sclerosis**
5. Joint inflammation is **mild** (unlike RA which is severely inflammatory)

**Primary OA** (idiopathic, age-related):
• Most common
• Affects **weight-bearing joints**: knees, hips, spine
• Also **DIPs** (Heberden nodes) and **PIPs** (Bouchard nodes)
• **NOT wrists, MCPs, elbows, ankles** (those = inflammatory arthritis until proven otherwise!)

**Secondary OA** (identifiable cause):
• Trauma (post-traumatic OA)
• Obesity (mechanical overload)
• Congenital deformity (hip dysplasia)
• Metabolic (hemochromatosis, acromegaly)
• Inflammatory joint disease (RA that damages joint → secondary OA)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Comparison grid: LEFT (OA): joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis. RIGHT (RA): erosions, juxta-articular osteopenia, symmetric involvement

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **OA vs RA on boards**: OA = **pain WITH use**, improves with rest. RA = pain **IMPROVES with use**, worse at rest with morning stiffness >30 min. OA has **crepitus** and **bony enlargement**; RA has **soft tissue swelling** and **warmth**. If a patient has OA, their ESR/CRP is NORMAL — if elevated, think inflammatory arthritis!

mnemonics.trigger: OA joints affected vs. RA joints

quick_checks.q: A 72-year-old woman has pain and bony swelling of DIP joints. ESR and CRP are normal. Most likely diagnosis?
quick_checks.explanation: Bony DIP enlargement = **Heberden nodes** = classic OA. Normal inflammatory markers rule out inflammatory arthritis like RA.

quick_checks.q: Which joint is LEAST likely affected by primary OA?
quick_checks.explanation: Wrists are typically affected by **RA**, not OA. OA classically affects DIP/PIP, knees, hips, and spine.

content_chunks.title: The Clinical Picture
content_chunks.content: Meet Carol: 66, retired teacher, BMI 31. She says her knees 'ache' after walking the mall but feel better after sitting for 10 minutes. Morning stiffness lasts about 15 minutes. She hears grinding when she bends her knees. On exam: bony enlargement at both knees, crepitus with flexion, and mild varus deformity. No warmth, no erythema. This is textbook OA — mechanical pain, short AM stiffness, crepitus, and bony changes.
content_chunks.visual_desc: Clinical photo showing bilateral knee bony enlargement with mild genu varum (bow-legged deformity)

content_chunks.title: Clinical Criteria for OA Diagnosis
content_chunks.content:
**Diagnosis is CLINICAL** — X-ray confirms but isn't always needed!

**ACR Clinical Criteria for Knee OA**:
• **Knee pain** most days of prior month
• **PLUS** 3 of these:
  → Age >50
  → Morning stiffness <30 minutes
  → Crepitus on active motion
  → Bony tenderness
  → Bony enlargement
  → No palpable warmth

**X-Ray Findings** (the 'OA Tetrad'):
1. **Joint space narrowing** (earliest sign — usually medial compartment in knee)
2. **Osteophytes** (bone spurs — MOST SPECIFIC for OA!)
3. **Subchondral sclerosis** (increased bone density under cartilage)
4. **Subchondral cysts** (fluid-filled cavities in bone)

**X-Ray Grade (Kellgren-Lawrence)**:
• **Grade 1**: Doubtful narrowing, possible osteophytes
• **Grade 2**: Definite osteophytes, possible narrowing
• **Grade 3**: Moderate osteophytes, definite narrowing, sclerosis
• **Grade 4**: Large osteophytes, severe narrowing, bone deformity
content_chunks.visual_desc: Four-panel X-ray progression: Grade 1 (mild narrowing) → Grade 2 (osteophytes) → Grade 3 (moderate narrowing + sclerosis) → Grade 4 (severe, bone-on-bone)

content_chunks.title: Differential Diagnosis: OA vs. Inflammatory Arthritis
content_chunks.content:
**OA** (Degenerative):
✅ Pain **worse with activity**, better with rest
✅ Morning stiffness **<30 min**
✅ **Bony** enlargement
✅ **Crepitus** common
✅ **Normal** ESR/CRP
✅ Unilateral or asymmetric

**RA** (Autoimmune):
🔴 Pain **worse at rest**, better with use
🔴 Morning stiffness **>30 min** (often >1 hour)
🔴 **Soft tissue** swelling
🔴 **Warm**, tender joints
🔴 **Elevated** ESR, CRP, RF, anti-CCP
🔴 **Symmetric** (same joints both sides)
🔴 Affects **wrists, MCPs, PIPs** (spares DIPs!)

**Gout** (Crystal):
🔴 **Acute**, intense pain
🔴 **Monoarticular** (classically 1st MTP)
🔴 **Erythema + warmth** (looks infected!)
🔴 Elevated uric acid
🔴 Resolves in 5-10 days untreated

**Pseudogout** (CPPD):
🔴 Acute or chronic
🔴 **Knees, wrists** most common
🔴 Seen with hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism
🔴 Chondrocalcinosis on X-ray (calcium in cartilage)
content_chunks.visual_desc: Side-by-side chart: OA (bony, crepitus, no warmth) vs RA (swollen, warm, symmetric) vs Gout (red, hot, 1st MTP)

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **Lab workup for OA = almost nothing!** OA is diagnosed clinically and with X-ray. Don't routinely order ESR, CRP, or RF in suspected OA with no red flags. But order labs if: joint is warm/erythematous (rule out infection/gout), symptoms are bilateral symmetric (rule out RA), or there's constitutional symptoms (fever, weight loss).

quick_checks.q: Which X-ray finding is MOST specific for osteoarthritis?
quick_checks.explanation: **Osteophytes** (bone spurs) are the MOST SPECIFIC radiographic finding for OA. Joint space narrowing is sensitive but not specific.

quick_checks.q: A patient has knee pain with morning stiffness lasting 45 minutes. ESR is 45. What is more likely?
quick_checks.explanation: Morning stiffness >30 minutes + elevated ESR indicates **inflammatory arthritis** (like RA), not OA. OA has stiffness <30 minutes and normal inflammatory markers.

content_chunks.title: Stepwise OA Management (ACR 2020 Guidelines)
content_chunks.content:
**ALWAYS start with non-pharmacologic. Meds are adjunctive!**

**Step 1: Foundation (ALL patients)**
✅ **Weight loss** → 1 lb lost = 4 lbs pressure off knees! 
   • 5% weight loss = 10% improvement in pain
   • 10% weight loss = 50% improvement!
✅ **Exercise** → Strongest evidence for quad strengthening
   • Low-impact: walking, swimming, cycling, tai chi
   • NOT high-impact running or jumping
✅ **Physical therapy** → quadriceps strengthening, gait training
✅ **Activity modification** → avoid stairs, kneeling; use cane in OPPOSITE hand

**Step 2: Topical (mild-moderate pain)**
✅ **Topical NSAIDs** (diclofenac gel 1%): FIRST-LINE for knee/hand OA
   • Effective as oral NSAIDs for knee OA
   • No systemic side effects (safer in elderly!)
✅ **Topical capsaicin**: alternative for patients who can't use NSAIDs

**Step 3: Oral (moderate-severe pain)**
✅ **Acetaminophen** ≤3000 mg/day (weak effect, but safe if no liver disease)
✅ **Oral NSAIDs** (naproxen, ibuprofen, meloxicam, celecoxib)
   • Most effective for OA pain
   • **Naproxen** 500 mg BID = lowest CV risk among NSAIDs
   • **Celecoxib** (COX-2 selective) = less GI bleeding, same CV risk
   • ALWAYS add **PPI** (omeprazole 20 mg daily) if age >60 or GI risk
   • Check renal function before starting (Cr, GFR)
✅ **Duloxetine** 30-60 mg daily: SNRI for chronic OA pain
   • Good option for patients with contraindications to NSAIDs
   • Also treats comorbid depression/chronic pain

**Step 4: Intra-articular (persistent pain despite oral meds)**
✅ **Corticosteroid injection** (triamcinolone, methylprednisolone)
   • Works in 1-3 days, lasts 4-12 weeks
   • **Max 3-4 per year** (can accelerate cartilage loss!)
✅ **Hyaluronic acid** (viscosupplementation) — controversial evidence
   • Medicare covers, but ACR conditionally recommends AGAINST

**Step 5: Surgical (severe, refractory)**
✅ **Total joint arthroplasty** (hip or knee replacement)
   • Best for end-stage OA with severe pain and functional limitation
   • Refer when: pain disrupts sleep, can't walk 2 blocks, fails conservative Rx
content_chunks.mnemonic: **OA Stepped Care = WET CAD**: **W**eight loss, **E**xercise, **T**opicals → **C**elecoxib/NSAIDs, **A**cetaminophen, **D**uloxetine → injection → surgery
content_chunks.visual_desc: Stepwise pyramid: Base = weight loss + exercise + PT (largest box). Tier 2 = topicals. Tier 3 = oral meds (NSAIDs, acetaminophen, duloxetine). Tier 4 = injections. Top = surgery (smallest)

content_chunks.title: NSAID Selection & Safety (Board Gold)
content_chunks.content:
**NSAID Comparison (High-Yield for Boards)**:

**Naproxen 500 mg BID**
• Best CV safety profile among non-selective NSAIDs
• Moderate GI risk
• OTC available

**Ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID**
• Most commonly used
• Short half-life (good for PRN use)
• Interferes with aspirin cardioprotection!

**Meloxicam 7.5-15 mg daily**
• Once-daily dosing (compliance!)
• Moderate selectivity

**Celecoxib 100-200 mg BID**
• **COX-2 selective** — less GI bleeding
• SAME CV risk as other NSAIDs
• Contraindicated in sulfa allergy

**Diclofenac 50 mg TID**
• Most hepatotoxic NSAID (watch LFTs)
• Also available as topical gel

**Safety Monitoring**:
✅ Check **Cr, GFR** before starting (recheck in 2-4 weeks if elderly)
✅ Check **LFTs** if using diclofenac
✅ **PPI** (omeprazole 20 mg) for anyone >60 or with GI risk
✅ Avoid NSAIDs if: CKD stage 3+, CHF, recent GI bleed, on anticoagulants
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 🔥 **Naproxen is the safest NSAID for CV risk?** Yes! Naproxen has the lowest cardiovascular risk of all NSAIDs. Ibuprofen and diclofenac have higher CV risk. Celecoxib (COX-2) has the same CV risk as other NSAIDs — don't assume it's safer for the heart (it's safer for the stomach).

content_chunks.title: Joint Injection: When & How
content_chunks.content:
**Indications**:
• Moderate-severe OA pain not controlled with oral meds
• Acute exacerbation of OA pain
• Bridge while awaiting surgery

**Contraindications**:
• Overlying skin infection or cellulitis
• Joint prosthesis (refer to ortho!)
• Uncontrolled coagulopathy or anticoagulation (relative)
• Bacteremia or sepsis
• Joint instability (injection won't help)

**Knee Injection Technique**:
1. **Position**: Patient supine, knee slightly flexed (pillow under knee)
2. **Landmark**: Lateral approach — needle goes under patella, between patella and femur
3. **Prep**: Chlorhexidine or betadine × 30 sec dry time
4. **Needle**: 22-25 gauge, 1.5 inch
5. **Aspirate** first (if effusion, drain it)
6. **Inject**: Triamcinolone 40 mg (or methylprednisolone 40 mg) mixed with 1-2 mL lidocaine
7. **Remove needle**, pressure, bandage
8. **Post-injection**: Rest for 24-48 hours, ice, no high-impact activity for 1 week

**Expected Response**: Pain relief in 24-72 hours, lasting 4-12 weeks
content_chunks.clinical_pearl: 🔥 **Don't inject through cellulitis!** If skin over knee is red/warm, DON'T inject — could seed bacteria into joint causing septic arthritis (orthopedic emergency!). Always examine injection site first.

content_chunks.content: 🔥 **What about glucosamine/chondroitin?** ACR **strongly recommends AGAINST** them — no better than placebo in large trials. Same for glucosamine, chondroitin, MSM, and most 'joint supplements.' Save your patients' money!

mnemonics.mnemonic: **OA Stepped Care = WET CAD**: **W**eight loss, **E**xercise, **T**opicals → **C**elecoxib/NSAIDs, **A**cetaminophen, **D**uloxetine → injection → surgery

quick_checks.q: First-line pharmacologic treatment for mild-moderate knee OA in a 70-year-old?
quick_checks.explanation: Topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel) are FIRST-LINE for mild-moderate knee/hand OA per ACR guidelines. Effective as oral NSAIDs with minimal systemic side effects — safer in elderly!

quick_checks.q: Which NSAID has the LOWEST cardiovascular risk?
quick_checks.explanation: **Naproxen** has the lowest CV risk profile among all NSAIDs. Ibuprofen and diclofenac interfere with aspirin's antiplatelet effect and have higher CV risk.

quick_checks.q: Patient with severe knee OA failed all conservative care. Pain keeps her up at night. What's next?
quick_checks.explanation: Pain disrupting sleep + failed conservative therapy = refer for **joint replacement** (TKA). Opioids are NOT recommended for chronic OA pain per ACR guidelines.
